Be honest. Lying on your résumé is never a good idea. Many people who lie on their applications end up losing their jobs when their employers find out the truth.

Top 10 Cover Letter Tips
Do your homework. Learn what you can about the company or organization you’re applying to, so you can tailor your cover letter and really show the employer that you could be a good fit.

Presentation counts. Use a font that’s easy to read, like 12-point Times New Roman, Calibri or Arial. Using 8.5 x 11-inch white paper is usually a smart choice.

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: Job: A piece of work, especially one done for hire or profit; a paid position of employment

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: Occupation: A person's usual or principal work or business, especially as a means of earning a living; vocation

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: Profession: A vocation or calling, especially one that involves some branch of advanced learning or science

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: Career: One’s advancement through life, especially in a profession; a profession or occupation, especially as offering advancement

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: By: Alison Doyle - thebalancecareers.com

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: When you're in high school and haven't worked much or at all, it can be hard to find a job. In fact, teenagers have a really high unemployment rate.

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: There are a few reasons why finding work as a teenager can be challenging:

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: Experience: If you're looking for your first job, you may not be able to easily show you have the necessary skills and experience.

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: Hours: Sometimes employers need candidates who can work late nights or during school hours, which may not be doable for students.

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: Personal qualities: Interviewers may feel concerned that teenagers lack responsibility, maturity, and other key personal qualities needed to perform in the role.

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: But don't get discouraged by these factors. There are plenty of things you can do to overcome those obstacles, get your application noticed, and get yourself hired:

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx

items.excerpt: Apply for Lots of Jobs

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: Job searching is a numbers game. Apply for as many jobs as possible. The more applications you have in, the better your chances are of securing an interview.

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: Keep applying for jobs, rather than waiting to hear back from one before you try for another position.

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: Be prepared to complete a job application. Bring all the information you need when you’re applying for jobs online and have the details handy when you’re filling out online job applications.

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: Spend as much time as you can applying and follow up by calling or emailing to check on your application. It will show that you’re actively job searching and interested in the position.

items.excerpt: If your job search seems to be going slowly and has become a tedious process, consider the following to aid in lifting your spirits:

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx

items.excerpt: Employers use job application forms as a screening tool to decide who they will interview. You can influence whether or not you eventually get hired by how you fill out the form.

items.excerpt: Ask for 2 copies of the application form. Use one for a draft and one for a final copy. If you can’t get an extra form, use a piece of paper to write a draft. Copy the draft information to the form.

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: Who is responsible for creating and maintaining a safe and healthy workplace?

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: Alberta’s Occupational Health and Safety Act is based on the idea that the primary responsibility for occupational health and safety is shared by everyone connected with that workplace — including employers, employees, c

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: What are the main responsibilities of employers?

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: Employers must take every reasonable precaution to ensure the health and safety of persons at or near the workplace. As an employer, some of your main responsibilities include:

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: providing and maintaining equipment with proper safety devices

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: providing employees with the training, information and supervision they need to do their jobs safely, including informing employees about any health or safety hazards in the workplace

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: making sure employees wear personal protective equipment and know how to use it properly

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: establishing a Joint Occupational Health and Safety Committee or ensuring that a Health and Safety Representative is selected, where required by legislation.

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: co-operating with the Joint Occupational Health and Safety Committee or Health and Safety Representative and with Health and Safety Officers from the Department of Labour

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: preparing and maintaining an occupational health and safety policy and/or program, where required by legislation.

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: preparing a list of hazardous chemicals present in the workplace

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: following the Occupational Health and Safety Act and regulations and making sure that employees also follow them

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: reporting anything in the workplace that may be dangerous

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: co-operating with the employer and fellow employees to protect health and safety

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: wearing personal protective equipment and following safety procedures

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: co-operating with the Joint Occupational Health and Safety Committee or Health and Safety Representative and with Health and Safety Officers from the Department of Labor

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx

items.excerpt: WHMIS stands for Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System.

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: It is an information system implemented in 1988 and modified in 2015, that is designed to help students know more about safety and health hazards of materials that they use in the workplace.

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: WHMIS gives workers and employers key safety and handling information in the form of special labels, symbols, and Material Safety Data Sheets (MSDS) on potentially dangerous chemicals that are used on the job.

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: You will come across controlled products that fall under the WHMIS legislation at school (for example, the chemicals used in your science and shop class), and at any workplace where chemicals are used.

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: All controlled products at school or the workplace must have WHMIS labels.

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: The purpose of a WHMIS label is to identify the product as controlled and alert workers or handlers to the hazards and safe handling procedures of the product. A WHMIS label is just a first alert, as the amount of inform

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: It is important that you read the whole label before using a product for the first time. The label will give a brief summary of the most important things to know about the chemical.

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: Name of the chemical: may be the common name, trade name, generic name, brand name, code name.

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: The WHMIS hazard symbols: hazard symbols representing the WHMIS hazard classes.

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: Risks and precautions: Short phrases describing the hazards to supplement the information provided by the symbols, and precautions to be taken when using, handling or being exposed to the product.

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: First Aid instructions: These statements indicate immediate first aid measures that can be taken by the victim or others in case of an accident or emergency.

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: Fire and explosive hazard - how easily it catches on fire or explodes.

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: Reactivity data - describes how it reacts with other chemicals

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: Toxicological properties - describes how it affects human health

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: Preventive measures to be taken

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: First aid measures to be taken if exposed

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: When it was made and who to contact for more information

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: Employers must keep the MSDS up to date (no older than three years) and on file at the worksite and must allow employees to read them and make copies of them.

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: The employer must educate workers about important information on the sheet for each chemical.

items.excerpt: Look out for these symbols on household chemical products to make sure you understand the dangers each product may pose to you or your home.

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: The second part of a hazard symbol is the frame, which tells you what part of the product is dangerous. There are two different frames you could see on a product label:

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: The container is dangerous. If a hazard symbol is in a triangular frame, it means the container can become dangerous if the product is stored improperly or misused. You’ll usually see an explosive symbol within a triangu

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: The contents are dangerous. If a hazard symbol is in an octagon frame, it means the product inside the container is dangerous. You’ll usually see a corrosive, flammable, or poisonous symbol within an octagon frame.

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: The third and final part of a hazard symbol is the caution signal, which explains the severity of the danger a product may pose. There are three different caution words you might see below a hazard symbol:

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: Caution means a product may cause temporary injury or even death if you have extreme prolonged exposure to the product.

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: Danger means a product may cause temporary injury, permanent injury, or death.

items.document: CALM Module 3  - Career and Life Choices.docx
items.excerpt: Extreme danger means exposure to even very small amounts of a product may cause serious injury or death.
